title: The serpent's question (Genesis 3:1–7)
hook: did God really say? the fruit, the eyes opened, the fig leaves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first not good in the Bible, a person with no one beside them, and your line was not good to be alone. Who did you reach out to? Day three hundred thirty-eight.

The most dangerous sentences don't always sound like lies. Sometimes they sound like questions. Are you sure your friend meant it that way? Didn't your boss technically say you could? Is that really what the doctor told you? A good question opens a door. A twisted one leaves a crack of doubt in something you trusted, and walks away. In the garden, everything is good. Two people, side by side, naked and not ashamed. And then, in the third chapter, a new voice arrives. It doesn't start with a command, or a threat. It starts with a question.
screen: `A LIE CAN SOUND LIKE A QUESTION.` → `A CRACK OF DOUBT.` → `A NEW VOICE IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening in the King James Bible: "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" Look how clever that is. God had said: eat freely of every tree, except one. The serpent turns a whole garden of yes into a single no. And in Hebrew there's a pun. Subtil, crafty, is arum. One verse earlier, the man and woman were arummim, naked. Naked and crafty, side by side. The woman answers, and adds something God never said: neither shall ye touch it. Then the serpent says it plainly: "Ye shall not surely die." And the fruit looks good, and pleasant, and wise-making, and she eats, and gives some to her husband, who, the text says, was with her. Then: "the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons." Two things the story doesn't say. It never says apple. That came much later, in European art; some think a Latin pun helped, since malum means both apple and evil. And Genesis never names the serpent as Satan. Many Christians read it that way, following the book of Revelation, which calls the devil that old serpent. Jewish readers have often read the story differently. But every reading notices how it began: not with a lie, but with a question that bent a good word.
screen: `A GARDEN OF YES BECOMES ONE NO.` · `ARUM AND ARUMMIM: CRAFTY, NAKED.` · `EYES OPENED, FIG LEAVES SEWN.` · `NO APPLE, NO NAME.` · then, large: `YEA, HATH GOD SAID?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a voice that twists good words. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days. Was there a voice, a headline, an ad, a comment, or the voice in your own head, that took something good and bent it into a question? You're not really loved. You can't actually trust them. Did they really mean it? Just notice it. Don't argue with it yet. Name it for what it is: a question that twists. If you pray, you can hold it up to God. The bell holds the time.
The serpent's question. Hath God said? The first temptation in the Bible starts with a question that turns a garden of yes into one no.
Your line: did god really say? Today, when a voice twists something good into doubt, notice it, and go back to what was actually said. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christian traditions read Genesis 3 at the start of Lent, and Christians of many churches speak of resisting temptation by returning to what scripture actually says, as Jesus does in the wilderness.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: Genesis says the fruit was an apple
it never says. the apple came later, in European art; a Latin pun may have helped.
Genesis 3 names the serpent as Satan
Genesis doesn't. many Christians read it that way, following Revelation's 'that old serpent'.
the text says the man was with the woman when she ate
she "gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat."

fork.setup: the serpent asks: "yea, hath God said, ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" you're the woman. what's true?
options: God said eat freely, except from one tree.
fork.reveal: a whole garden of yes, with one no. the question's trick is to make the one no look like everything.

original.note: Hebrew: crafty, shrewd. It echoes arummim, naked, one verse before.

trapdoor: what you thought: the devil, disguised as a snake, tempted Eve with an apple.
what it means: a crafty voice asks a question that bends a good word, and trust cracks.
what a scholar hears: arum and arummim, a pun on crafty and naked; no apple and no Satan in Genesis itself; those come from later reading.

notes: arum (3:1) / arummim (2:25) wordplay is widely noted; confirm.
Apple and the Latin pun malum/malum: the pun is often suggested; script says 'some think'. Confirm.
Christian identification of the serpent with Satan via Revelation 12:9 and 20:2; Jewish readings described only as 'often read the story differently'. Confirm this is fair and sufficient.
'Many Christian traditions read Genesis 3 at the start of Lent' (howItsDone): e.g. Revised Common Lectionary Lent 1, Year A. Confirm wording.
